headline: Parliament Advances Youth Boot Camp Bill Amid Clashes Over Homelessness and Student Costs
summary: Parliament advanced legislation enabling military-style youth justice orders, despite opposition warnings that the approach could deepen harm and fail to reduce reoffending. Question Time also exposed disputes over rising homelessness, student living costs, ministerial standards and a new oil and gas exploration permit. MPs passed the English Language Bill and advanced reforms to building-trade licensing, while debate began on a competition law bill.

topicSummaries.topic: Homelessness Data and Government Response Challenged
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Housing insecurity affects people’s access to safe, stable homes, while the debate raised questions about support for people leaving prison, hospitals and care.
topicSummaries.content: Green MP Tamatha Paul questioned Housing Minister Chris Bishop about Salvation Army findings that homelessness was increasing and about reported reductions in funding and transitional housing places. Bishop said he was concerned about homelessness, citing increases in severe housing deprivation, temporary accommodation and rough sleeping between 2018 and 2023, but argued the report’s findings were not a substitute for statistical data. He said the Government had delivered more than 8,000 social homes since November 2023 and was funding a longer-term pipeline, while disputing some of Paul’s figures. Bishop also said it was a serious problem when people left prison or mental health facilities without a fixed home and said the system needed to change.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tamatha Paul (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he accept that 18 of 19 front-line providers told the Salvation Army that homelessness has increased over the last six months?

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: That is what the report says—yes.

topicSummaries.topic: Youth Boot Camp Bill Passes Second Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill could place some 14- to 17-year-olds convicted of serious offending in military-style programmes, with direct consequences for young people, their families and public safety.
topicSummaries.content: The Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill passed its second reading with support from National, ACT and New Zealand First, while Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed it. The bill creates a “young serious offender” declaration and allows military-style academy orders as a sentencing option. Opponents argued that evidence from the pilot and past programmes did not show reduced reoffending, and raised concerns about trauma, Māori overrepresentation, use of force and safeguards left to later regulations. Government supporters said the measure targets a small group of repeat serious offenders and combines consequences with rehabilitation and protection for the public.

keyExchanges.speaker: Jenny Salesa (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Seven out of 10 young people who went through this Government’s military-style academy pilot reoffended, and most of them within two months of coming home.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ryan Hamilton (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This is just another example of proactive, measured law and order and community safety that may well be the necessary intervention that these young people need.

topicSummaries.topic: Student Job and Living Costs Under Scrutiny
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Pressure on students’ food, housing and employment can affect whether they can continue studying and build a future in New Zealand.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Shanan Halbert challenged the Government over student living costs, citing a survey finding that 38 percent of Victoria University respondents had skipped a meal because of costs, and figures showing 434,000 applications for 53,000 Student Job Search positions. Acting tertiary education minister Chris Penk acknowledged that cost pressures had been challenging but pointed to lower recent rent inflation and food inflation of 2.8 percent, compared with 12.5 percent a few years earlier. He also cited student allowances, loans and other support, and argued that Government measures to encourage business and construction would help create jobs. Halbert additionally raised a reported 19 percent rise in tuition fees since 2024 and survey responses indicating some students were considering leaving the country.

keyExchanges.speaker: Shanan Halbert (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How can tertiary students succeed in their studies when a recent student survey at Victoria University found that 38 percent of students recently skipped a meal due to cost of living pressures?

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Penk (National)
keyExchanges.quote: No one is denying that cost of living pressures have been challenging for many New Zealanders over the last six years.

topicSummaries.topic: Ministerial Standards and Defence Force Flights Disputed
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The exchanges put public accountability, the use of taxpayer-funded travel and the Government’s response to controversial remarks under scrutiny.
topicSummaries.content: Labour Deputy Leader Carmel Sepuloni questioned acting Prime Minister David Seymour about remarks attributed to the Minister of Foreign Affairs concerning China and about a comment telling a Chinese-born New Zealander to return to their own country. Seymour disputed Sepuloni’s characterisation of the minister’s remarks and argued that parliamentary free speech applied. Sepuloni also challenged the Prime Minister’s use of Defence Force aircraft, including a reported flight costing more than $12,000 to save about 45 minutes travelling from Auckland to Hamilton; Seymour said he stood by the Government’s position that the flights imposed no additional cost. The Speaker declined Sepuloni’s request for an urgent debate on the Foreign Affairs Minister’s comments, ruling the matter was not immediately urgent.

keyExchanges.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he accept that a leader who breaks his own promise on air travel, and is too weak to discipline a Minister who tells a Chinese-born New Zealander to go back to his own country, has built a Government of no standards and no accountability?

keyExchanges.speaker: David Seymour (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: On behalf of the Prime Minister, what we’ve seen is an attempted orchestral conductorship, where she’s built up the questions and she’s tried to really rise to a cacophony, a triumph, and unfortunately, the way question time’s gone today, she just hit a bum note.

topicSummaries.topic: $604M Pharmac Uplift and Cancer Services Investment Outlined
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The announced funding and service changes aim to expand access to cancer medicines, diagnosis and treatment, including care closer to home.
topicSummaries.content: Health Minister Simeon Brown outlined Government measures across the cancer pathway, including a $604 million uplift to Pharmac that he said funded 66 new medicines, 33 of them cancer treatments. He also cited $210 million to expand cancer treatment services and infusion capacity and $65 million for diagnostic procedures. Brown said a new linear accelerator was treating patients at Wellington Regional Hospital, with further equipment and services planned or under development elsewhere. He also described plans to extend breast screening to women aged 70 to 74 and to lower the bowel screening age to 56 as an initial step towards alignment with Australia.

topicSummaries.topic: English Language Bill Passes Final Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law formally recognises English as an official language, while the debate raised questions about Parliament’s priorities and the status of te reo Māori and New Zealand Sign Language.
topicSummaries.content: The English Language Bill passed its third reading with support from National, ACT and New Zealand First; Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed it. Minister Casey Costello said the bill formalised English’s official status and did not change existing protections for te reo Māori or New Zealand Sign Language. Opponents argued English already functioned as an official language and that the legislation offered little practical effect while using parliamentary time that could be spent on other issues. The debate also exposed disagreement over whether the bill was a straightforward clarification or a politically divisive measure.

keyExchanges.speaker: Casey Costello (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill provides clarity and certainty in legislation of the status of the English language in New Zealand.

keyExchanges.speaker: Camilla Belich (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: There is no need for this bill, and it is regretful, when there are so many challenging issues facing New Zealand, that this is the issue that the Government has chosen to focus on.

topicSummaries.topic: Building Trades Licensing Bill Wins Cross-Party Support
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The reforms are intended to strengthen oversight of building and trade work, giving consumers clearer ways to raise concerns about work in their homes.
topicSummaries.content: The Building and Construction Sector (Strengthening Occupational Licensing Regimes) Amendment Bill passed its second reading after support from across the House. It changes licensing and disciplinary systems for building practitioners, electricians, plumbers, gasfitters and drainlayers, including giving regulators stronger investigative powers and keeping records of cancelled licences on a public register for three years. Changes recommended by the select committee include raising the maximum fine for licensed building practitioners from $10,000 to $20,000 and the maximum suspension from 12 to 24 months. MPs broadly supported improved consumer protections, while debate continued over potential costs and how professional codes of ethics should be applied.

keyExchanges.speaker: Simon Court (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: Some people’s version of ethics is actually “wokery”.

keyExchanges.speaker: Duncan Webb (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: If we want more, for example, women or Pasifika tradies, then we need to make sure that their workplaces are safe.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Announces 12-Year Oil and Gas Permit
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The permit could affect future domestic energy supply, with potential consequences for households and businesses reliant on gas.
topicSummaries.content: Resources Minister Shane Jones said a 12-year petroleum permit had been allocated following the removal of the oil and gas exploration ban. He argued that declining gas supply was affecting industrial firms and said a previously announced $200 million fund would soon produce decisions. The announcement drew criticism and interjections from Labour MPs, including former energy minister Megan Woods, while Jones blamed the previous Government’s policy for damage to Taranaki. No further details of the permit’s expected production or effect on household energy costs were provided in the exchange.

keyExchanges.speaker: Shane Jones (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: A 12-year petroleum permit has been allocated after the ban has been removed, a ban that has had ruinous consequences upon the region of Taranaki.

keyExchanges.speaker: Megan Woods (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why did you email asking to come, then?

topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes could affect how businesses merge or collaborate and how effectively regulators can respond to competition problems that influence prices and consumer choice.
topicSummaries.content: Commerce Minister Cameron Brewer began the second-reading debate on the Commerce (Promoting Competition and Other Matters) Amendment Bill, which had not reached a vote when the sitting ended. The bill proposes changes to merger rules, allows the High Court to order corrective action for breaches, and creates a process for businesses to seek approval for certain conduct. Amendments following select committee scrutiny removed proposed new market-study powers and revised other provisions to address concerns about business certainty and the Commerce Commission’s role. The debate was interrupted and set down for resumption at the next sitting.

conclusion: The House advanced major legislation, but the day’s sharpest disputes centred on whether the Government’s approaches to youth offending, housing insecurity and cost pressures will deliver practical results without creating further harm.
